title: Comparing the forms: establishment, management and funding
summary: One revision page that lines up every form in the deck on how it is established, how it is managed and how it is funded.

chunks.heading: How each form is established
chunks.explanation_md:
Use this as your answer frame for **establishment**.

- **Sole proprietorship**: minimum formalities; local registration may be needed depending on state and city; no audit needed.
- **Partnership**: oral or written agreement; a written **partnership deed** sets out the terms.
- **LLP**: a five-step registration, from DSC to filing the LLP agreement.
- **Private limited company**: Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association and Certificate of Incorporation; may commence business immediately after incorporation.
- **Public limited company**: the same incorporation route, but it also needs a **certificate of commencement** from the Registrar, and a prospectus before raising capital.
- **Cooperative society**: members with a common background come together under the Indian Co-operative Societies Act 1912.
- **Trust**: at least two trustees, registered with the Charity Commissioner.
- **Society**: at least seven individuals, registered with the Registrar of Societies, with memorandum and rules.
- **Section 8 company**: at least three individuals, applying to the Regional Director of the Company Law Board.
chunks.exam_line: Establishment ranges from minimum formalities (sole proprietor) to registration with the Registrar of Companies (company), Charity Commissioner (trust), Registrar of Societies (society).

chunks.heading: How each form is managed
chunks.explanation_md:
Use this as your answer frame for **management**.

- **Sole proprietorship**: the owner is taxed in his personal capacity.
- **Partnership**: the deed names who has authority to manage the firm and sign cheques, and how tasks are divided; unlimited liability.
- **Joint stock company**: shareholders elect a **Board of Directors**, which hires the senior management; independent directors act as a watchdog.
- **Cooperative society**: run by the members themselves.
- **Trust**: governed by its **trustees**, who hold legal title and may not delegate discretionary duties.
- **Society**: managed by an elected **governing council or managing committee**; members have voting rights.
- **Section 8 company**: governed by directors, a managing committee or governing council elected by members, similar to a society.
chunks.exam_line: Management: owner (sole), partners per deed, board of directors (company), members (cooperative), trustees (trust), managing committee (society, Section 8).

chunks.heading: How each form is funded and how long it lasts
chunks.explanation_md:
Use this as your answer frame for **funding and continuity**.

- **Sole proprietorship**: a balance sheet helps when seeking a bank loan; ends with the entrepreneur's death.
- **Partnership**: partners voluntarily combine their capital; a balance sheet is advisable for raising a loan; no continuity.
- **Private limited company**: no invitation to the public; shares held by directors and members; minimum paid-up capital one lakh rupees; two to two hundred shareholders.
- **Public limited company**: minimum paid-up capital five lakh rupees; raises part of its capital through a **public offering** on stock exchanges; perpetual succession.
- **Cooperative society**: members combine their capital to serve themselves, since individually they have too little.
- **Not-for-profit forms**: no restriction on business activities, but profits must go fully to charitable objects (else tax at 35.1%); to be tax-exempt they must spend 85% of income on their objects.
chunks.exam_line: Funding: owner and bank loan (sole), partners' pooled capital (partnership), members only (private), public offering (public), members' pooled capital (cooperative), charitable use of profits (NPOs).

questions.stem: Compare sole proprietorship and partnership on establishment, taxation and continuity.
questions.model_answer_md:
Both are simple, lightly regulated forms, but they differ.

- **Establishment**: a sole proprietorship has minimum formalities (local registration only in some places); a partnership starts by an oral or written agreement, usually a deed.
- **People and capital**: one owner versus two or more people (up to fifty) combining capital.
- **Taxation**: a sole proprietor is taxed individually and the business is not taxed separately.
- **Continuity**: neither has continuity; a sole proprietorship dissolves on the entrepreneur's death and a partnership on a partner's death, retirement or insolvency.
- **Audit**: not necessary in either.

rubric.point: Establishment: minimum formalities versus agreement or deed
One owner versus two to fifty partners

questions.stem: Compare a private limited company and a cooperative society on funding.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Private limited company**: no invitation to the public for shares, debentures or deposits; capital comes from members, directors or their relatives; minimum paid up capital one lakh rupees; liability limited to investment.

**Cooperative society**: members combine capital to serve the members rather than to create profits, because individually they have inadequate capital.

So the company is funded by shareholders with a share capital, while the cooperative pools members' capital to serve themselves.

rubric.point: Private company: closed funding from members, directors, relatives

questions.stem: Compare sole proprietorship, partnership and joint stock company on how each is established, managed and funded.
questions.model_answer_md:
The deck lists sole proprietorship, partnership and joint stock company among the four commercial forms. They differ on establishment, management and funding.

| Basis | Sole proprietorship | Partnership | Joint stock company |
|---|---|---|---|
| Establishment | Minimum formalities; local registration in some places | Oral or written agreement; deed sets terms | Memorandum and Articles of Association, Certificate of Incorporation, Registrar of Companies |
| Management | The owner, taxed personally | Partners per the deed, with named authority to manage and sign cheques | Board of Directors elected by shareholders, hiring senior management |
| Funding | Owner; balance sheet helps for a bank loan | Partners combine capital; balance sheet advisable for a loan | Shareholders' capital; a public company can use a public offering |
| Liability | Not described | Unlimited | Limited to the shareholders' investment |
| Continuity | None; ends on death | None; ends on a partner's death, retirement or insolvency | Perpetual succession |
| Legal identity | Owner taxed individually | Firm with partners | Artificial person, separate legal entity |

**Public versus private company.** A private company cannot invite the public; a public company needs a prospectus, a certificate of commencement and can be listed.

In conclusion, as one moves from sole proprietorship to company, formalities, management structure and access to funds all increase, and continuity improves.

rubric.point: Separate legal entity of a company

questions.stem: A group of friends wants to start a business and is choosing between a partnership, a private limited company and a cooperative society. Advise them on how each would be established, managed and funded.
questions.model_answer_md:
The deck gives each form its own set-up, management and funding.

**Partnership.**
- *Establishment*: an oral or written agreement; a deed names the firm, partners and contributions.
- *Management*: as the deed says, including who manages and signs cheques.
- *Funding*: partners combine their capital; unlimited liability; no continuity.

**Private limited company.**
- *Establishment*: DSC, DIN, name check, eMoA and eAoA, PAN and TAN, Registrar certificate and a bank account; may commence right after incorporation.
- *Management*: a Board of Directors elected by shareholders.
- *Funding*: from members, directors or relatives, with minimum one lakh rupees paid up capital, two to two hundred shareholders; liability limited to investment; perpetual succession.

**Cooperative society.**
- *Establishment*: members with a common background under the Indian Co-operative Societies Act 1912.
- *Management*: run by the members.
- *Funding*: members combine capital to serve themselves rather than create profits; limited liability and perpetual succession.

**Advice.** If they want profits shared by deed with the least formality, a partnership fits but ends if a partner leaves. If they want limited liability and continuity with closed funding, a private limited company fits. If their aim is mutual service rather than profit, a cooperative fits.

In conclusion, the choice depends on liability, continuity and whether the goal is profit or member service.

questions.stem: Compare the commercial forms with the not-for-profit forms (trust, society, Section 8 company) on establishment, management and use of profits.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Commercial forms** (sole proprietorship, partnership, joint stock company, cooperative society) are built for business, while **not-for-profit forms** must apply profits to charitable objects.

| Basis | Trust | Society | Section 8 company | Joint stock company |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Establishment | At least two trustees; Charity Commissioner of the state | At least seven individuals; Registrar of Societies | At least three individuals; Regional Director of the Company Law Board | Memorandum and Articles; Registrar of Companies |
| Management | Trustees | Elected managing committee | Directors or committee elected by members | Board of Directors |
| Property | Vests in trustees | In society's name | Held by the company | Company is a separate legal entity |
| Dissolution | Generally irrevocable | Allowed with three-fifths approval | Allowed | Wound up by legal procedure |
| Profits | Applied to charitable objects | Not distributed to members | Not distributed to members | Shared as dividends per the Articles' policy |

**Use of profits.** Not-for-profits can carry on business, but profits must go fully to charitable objects, or the tax exemption is lost and income is taxed at 35.1%. For exemption they must spend 85% of income on their objects.

In conclusion, the not-for-profit forms differ mainly in registration authority, who manages and what happens to surplus.

rubric.point: Profits not distributed to members; charitable use
